analysis.one_liner: Directs the government to negotiate Medicare drug prices with pharmaceutical companies, repealing the ban on doing so.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred to two House committees in March 2010, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, despite 81 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the 'non-interference' rule added when Medicare Part D was created in 2003, which forbids the government from negotiating drug prices. Instead, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would be required to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with drug manufacturers on behalf of the roughly 30 million seniors and disabled people enrolled in Medicare drug plans. Plans could still bargain for even lower prices, and the Secretary could not impose a specific formulary. The bill went to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who pay out of pocket for a share of drug costs and whose premiums and copays are tied to the prices plans pay; and by extension taxpayers, since Medicare subsidizes a large share of Part D costs.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the Part D 'non-interference' provision and directs the Secretary of HHS to negotiate the prices, discounts, and rebates drug manufacturers may charge Part D plans for their enrollees.
Requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations conducted and the prices and discounts achieved, creating public accountability for the results.
Preserves the existing formulary rules and leaves plans free to negotiate prices below the government-negotiated level, so plans cannot use the change to narrow beneficiaries' drug access.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose government-wide customer for prescription drugs would gain bargaining power it deliberately lacks today. Their shareholders, not patients or taxpayers, would bear the cost of lower prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not specify targets, benchmarks, or enforcement for the negotiation, so it would rely on the Secretary's diligence and could produce discounts well short of what government purchasing power suggests.

Critics of government negotiation argue it could evolve into price controls that reduce industry revenue available for developing new drugs, a tradeoff between lower costs today and future innovation.
Because it applies only to Part D prices for enrollees, it would not directly lower drug costs for people with private insurance or the uninsured.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the benefit is direct: drug prices are a major share of seniors' out-of-pocket health costs, and the largest single purchaser of prescription drugs in the world would finally be allowed to bargain. The main cost falls on drug manufacturers, though an honest caveat is that a negotiation mandate with no stated benchmarks could deliver less than promised, and the bill's effects would be limited to Medicare enrollees.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Health Subcommittee five days later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on March 3, 2010, with 81 original cosponsors, including 80 of the 253 House Democrats and one of the 178 House Republicans.

The bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee; on March 8, 2010 it was referred to a subcommittee on health, and the record shows no further action of any kind.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, with the bill still stalled in committee, so it died without any vote in either chamber.
The timing is notable: the Affordable Care Act was enacted weeks after introduction, in March 2010, and the Part D non-interference ban this bill would have repealed was left intact.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed in place for another twelve years, keeping Medicare as a customer that pays whatever plans and manufacturers charge. Millions of Medicare beneficiaries continued to pay the resulting prices.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 81 original cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.role: One of 178 House Republicans, original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the lone Republican.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.role: Committees of referral; their subcommittee on health and their chairs never scheduled action
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died in committee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: Fought government negotiation of Medicare drug prices, the policy this bill would have enacted, throughout the health care debate of 2009-2010.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 80 of 253 House Democrats cosigned versus 1 of 178 House Republicans, and no committee ever brought the bill up.

industries.note: Medicare Part D bars the government from negotiating drug prices, leaving drugmakers free to charge plans market prices for a vast, government-subsidized customer base. This bill would have removed that protection, and the industry's opposition is the reason the policy stayed off the table.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Plans would buy drugs at the government-negotiated price, cutting their drug costs, but the government would displace their role as the party that bargains with drugmakers. The bill expressly lets plans negotiate below the negotiated price and keeps their formulary duties intact.
